hook.text: You're reading this in a voice right now. That silent narrator in your head talks to you constantly.

buildup.text: Vygotsky proposed that inner speech develops from childhood self-talk that gradually goes underground.

discovery.text: Brain scans show that inner speech activates Broca's area—the same motor speech circuits used for talking aloud.

twist.text: Not everyone has inner speech. Some people think entirely in images or feelings, with no verbal narration.

climax.text: Inner speech helps with planning, self-control, and working memory. It's the brain talking to itself to stay organized.

punchline.text: The voice in your head is a cognitive tool, not a quirk.

quiz.question: Where does inner speech come from, according to Vygotsky?

details.summary: Inner speech is the voice in your head when you think in words. Vygotsky proposed it develops from external speech that children internalize. Brain imaging shows inner speech activates many of the same areas as overt speech.
details.whyItMatters: Inner speech is central to conscious experience. Understanding it illuminates self-control, auditory hallucinations, and the relationship between language and thought.
takeaways: Inner speech develops from externalized self-directed talk
It activates language production areas in the brain
It supports planning, self-regulation, and working memory

faq.question: Does everyone have inner speech?
faq.answer: Most people report inner speech, but the experience varies enormously. Some people think primarily in words; others think in images, feelings, or abstract non-verbal patterns. Research by Russell Hurlburt using experience sampling found surprising diversity in inner experience across individuals.

faq.question: Is inner speech related to auditory hallucinations?
faq.answer: Possibly. One theory is that auditory hallucinations in conditions like schizophrenia result from inner speech that is misattributed to an external source.
